text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Government support to a vocational training group is putting pressure on small businesses by keeping prices artificially low, according to one educational centre.

- Police received a bomb threat over the weekend in Malmo, at a shopping centre just metres from Prime Minister Goran Persson's home. The threat was the latest in a series from a previously unknown group called We Who Built Sweden, that accused the centre-left government of being responsible for damaging living conditions for the old, sick and unemployed with politicians and immigrants benefitting.
- A survey finds lower food prices and a better economy are the most important things for Swedes right now. Lower taxes and cheaper petrol came next in the list of Christmas wishes.

- The year 1996 has been one of headlines for drug company Astra's managing director Hakan Mogren but the company remains on track and the largest on the Stockholm bourse. Mogren in an interview with the newspaper says Astra has not heard a word from rumoured suitor Roche and has not thought of lifting its share of AMI despite continuous reports.

- Next year will be dramatic for Sweden's financial sector, says investment group Investor's managing director Claes Dahlback who expects to see a merger between big banks. Dahlback says the number of banks and insurance companies will be halved over the year.

- Analysts are bullish on ICB Shipping's performance on the bourse in 1997, according to the newspaper. They expect the bourse to rise 10-20 percent in the first six months of the year and see ICB as the favoured stock. This year the Stockholm general index has risen 36 percent while ICB has climbed 40 percent.
